analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes for owners of closely held corporations, their heirs, and executives deferring pay.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced with a single cosponsor in June 2024, it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite several tax rules for S corporations — closely held companies whose profits pass through to owners' personal tax returns. It would give the heirs of S corporation owners a new deduction for the company's built-in gains, let these companies hold far more passive income (rents, dividends, interest) without losing their tax status, allow foreign investors and IRAs to own S corporation stock, and repeal the federal rule (Section 409A) that forces executives to pay tax on deferred compensation when it vests. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of closely held S corporations and their heirs, executives with nonqualified deferred compensation arrangements, nonresident foreign investors, and self-directed IRA holders. These are predominantly wealthy households: S corporations are closely held businesses, and nonqualified deferred compensation plans are used almost exclusively by highly paid executives.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of closely held corporations and their heirs

how_it_helps.text: It creates a new deduction letting heirs of an S corporation owner amortize the company's built-in gain over 15 years when they inherit, with an accelerated deduction when inherited property is sold [S2].

It raises the limit on passive investment income (rents, royalties, dividends, interest) an S corporation can collect without a tax penalty from 25% of receipts to 60%, and repeals the rule that excessive passive income terminates S corporation status entirely [S2].

It repeals Section 409A of the tax code, the rule requiring deferred compensation to be included in income when it is no longer subject to risk of forfeiture, effectively letting employers and executives delay paying income tax on promised pay far into the future [S2].

It lets nonresident foreign individuals own S corporation stock, permits IRAs (including Roth IRAs) to hold S corporation shares, and treats all employees of a firm as a single shareholder for the 100-shareholder limit, which eases large transfers of company stock to employee stock ownership plans [S2].
It lets suspended business losses pass to a new owner when a shareholder dies, preserving deductions that currently die with the owner [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, through the revenue lost to the new deductions, the higher passive-income allowance, and the repeal of the deferred compensation rules.

drawbacks.text: Repealing Section 409A would let highly paid executives defer salary, bonus, and equity pay indefinitely and postpone income tax on it until withdrawal, instead of paying when the compensation vests — a revenue loss concentrated among the highest earners [S2].

The new built-in gain deduction and the transfer of suspended losses at death stack additional tax advantages on top of the existing step-up in basis at death, so appreciated business wealth would pass to heirs with several layers of relief [S2].

Allowing S corporations to collect up to 60% of receipts from rents, dividends, and interest blurs the line between operating businesses and passive investment holding vehicles that receive pass-through tax treatment [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow and overwhelmingly flow to owners of closely held businesses, their heirs, and top executives, while the cost is broad: less federal revenue that other taxpayers must make up. The Section 409A repeal is the most sweeping piece and is very difficult to defend on broad-benefit grounds; the passive income and estate provisions mainly loosen limits written to prevent S corporations from becoming tax shelters. The employee ownership provision in Section 5 is the only piece with a plausible broad constituency, and even that primarily eases transactions for selling owners.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a markup or hearing before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Wenstrup (R-OH) introduced the bill on June 4, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S4].
One Republican member cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S3].
No further action was ever taken: the action history ends with the June 4, 2024 referral, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off than under the bill: none of the tax breaks for closely held business owners, their heirs, or executives deferring pay took effect, and no revenue was lost. The bill's prospective beneficiaries gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; the proposed tax cuts never happened

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, and no Democrat publicly supported it.

industries.industry: Closely held S corporations and their owners
industries.note: The bill would give owners and their heirs major new tax advantages: a built-in gain deduction at death, permission to collect far more passive investment income, and preservation of suspended losses. The cost of these breaks would fall on federal revenue, which other taxpayers cover.

Repealing Section 409A would let executives postpone income tax on deferred salary, bonuses, and equity pay until far in the future, instead of when the pay vests. The benefit is concentrated among top earners and paid for by the Treasury.

The bill would open S corporation ownership to nonresident alien individuals for the first time, while imposing withholding on their share of U.S.-connected income. This expands access to a U.S. pass-through tax structure that was previously limited to citizens and residents.

industries.industry: ESOP trustees and employee-ownership service providers
industries.note: Treating all employees of a firm as one shareholder for the 100-shareholder limit would make it easier to sell large companies to employee stock ownership plans. Workers in those plans could gain real ownership stakes, though the provision also eases exits for the selling owners.
